summary:
Terra Chamando is a cooperative 2D game where a team designs a space mission on Earth and then flies it. Players go through the nine NASA Concept Maturity Levels (CML 1 to 9), from the “cocktail napkin” idea to the critical design review. Every choice about rocket, power, instruments, reserves and risks costs credits and changes the spacecraft. During the flight, those choices come back as consequences: unmitigated risks happen more often, a spare part can save the reactor, and good communications help the reentry.

One player is the scientist on Earth, using real solar-flare records from NASA DONKI to decide whether to warn the crew. It shows that space missions are decided long before launch, and that mission control and crew depend on each other.

Terra Chamando answers the Space Mission Design Game challenge by letting players plan and then run their own mission: they design it through the nine CML stages, launch it, fly it with a crew supported from Earth, and see in the final report how each design decision shaped the outcome.
details:
What It Does

The game covers a whole mission in seven phases: planning on Earth, crew roles, launch, operations, random events, return, and a final evaluation.

Up to four people can play together on a local network or over the internet (one player hosts from the desktop build), or one person can play alone and switch between astronaut and scientist.

Planning

The crew votes on the mission objective at CML 1. The remaining stages are split among the players. Along the way they choose the rocket, the power source and hull, the instrument kit and spare parts, the reserve policy, which inconsistencies to fix or accept (CML 6), which of the three biggest risks to mitigate (CML 7), and how to handle requirements that fail the preliminary design review (CML 8).

Credits are limited and never go negative. Choices change mass, fuel, energy use, schedule margin, reliability, communications, risk, spare parts and science capacity.

Operations

Players keep the crew alive (food, water, sleep, health, reactor core temperature), run a fungus bio-nutrient experiment, and fly to the Moon, Mars or Jupiter.

The values from planning feed directly into the trip. Every 30 seconds the game may trigger a communication blackout, an asteroid on a collision course, or a thermal failure in the reactor. The risks the crew accepted at CML 7 make the matching event more likely.

The Scientist’s Role

The scientist stays on Earth and has their own work: analysing samples with microscope and Petri dish minigames, solving formula problems, preparing reagents, forecasting hazards, and calculating asteroid impact times.

During a solar storm, the scientist reads the solar terminal and decides whether to alert the ship. If the alert is sent, the crew has 20 seconds to turn on the shields. A false alarm wastes energy and time, and ignoring a real storm costs health and scrambles the controls.

Return and Report

The crew checks the systems, chooses a return window and a reentry angle.

The game then produces a post-mission report with a score, a timeline of events, and a section that links each consequence back to the planning decision that caused it.

How It Works

All systems share one mission state. The host runs the simulation and clients receive a mirror of it.

Client requests are accepted only if the player’s role allows them, so, for example, only the scientist can decide the solar alert.

Each event in the report carries a label:

  • REAL: Based on a real scientific record.
  • RISK: Real phenomenon, simulated occurrence.
  • FICTIONAL: A challenge created for the game.

No fictional event is presented as NASA data.

Benefits and Goals

We want players to feel why missions need planning, trade-offs and teamwork, using the same vocabulary real teams use.

For this challenge, the key design choice is that planning is not a menu before the game: the decisions made in CML 1 to 9 become the parameters the flight uses, so the mission the team designs is the mission it has to survive.

The game is in Portuguese and English and includes a colour-name option for players who cannot tell colours apart.

Tools

  • Godot 4 and GDScript for the game.
  • ENet and WebSocket for multiplayer.
  • Python 3 for the NASA data script.
  • Git/GitHub.

The project includes an automated test suite (303 checks) and a multiplayer integration test for four players.

Current State

The planning phase, flight, solar storm, return, post-mission report and multiplayer are working.

Next steps:

  • More tasks and events.
  • A distinct engineer role.
  • More NASA data sources (NeoWs, EONET).
  • Mission objectives beyond the bio-nutrient experiment.
